summary: Discusses when it is appropriate to register and use an Autonomous System, and lists criteria for doing so. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Each big network that picks its own routes needs a special badge number. This note says when you really need one and when you do not.

subtitle: When a network really needs its own Autonomous System number, and when it is better off without one.

tldr.problem: Many sites asked for Autonomous System numbers just because it seemed part of connecting to the Internet, which wasted a finite number space and cluttered routing.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an AS as a connected group of IP prefixes with a single and clearly defined routing policy, and gives criteria and sample cases for deciding whether a network needs one.
tldr.outcome: The main rule: a multi-homed site is almost the only case where an operator should create its own AS. The RFC is a Best Current Practice that was later updated by RFC 6996 and RFC 7300.

facts.label: ASes actively routed at the time

today: RFC 1930 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 6) and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6996 and RFC 7300, so read it together with those. The numbers in it, such as the 16-bit AS space, reflect 1996.

sections.title: Why the Guidelines Were Written
sections.content:
RFC 1930 is aimed at network operators and service providers who need to understand when they should use an Autonomous System (AS). It assumes the reader knows routing protocols and configures Internet networks.

The authors say there was a great deal of confusion about how ASes should be used, and the memo tries to clear that up while acting as a simple guide to exterior routing. The AS is described as the unit of routing policy, which matters for protocols such as EGP, BGP and IDRP. At the time the RFC was written, BGP was the current de facto standard for routing between ASes.
sections.eli5: Lots of people were asking for badge numbers they did not need. This note is a handbook that explains who really needs one.

sections.title: What an Autonomous System Is
sections.content:
The RFC first fixes the word prefix: a block of networks written as an address and a mask, such as 192.168.0.0/22 standing for four /24 networks. A prefix is the same thing as a CIDR block.

It then restates the definition of an AS: a connected group of one or more IP prefixes run by one or more network operators which has a SINGLE and CLEARLY DEFINED routing policy. Routing policy is about exchanging routing information. For traffic to flow towards a prefix NET1 between two ASes, ASX must announce NET1 and ASY must accept it. Each side chooses freely what to announce and what to accept.

Policies are set for groups of prefixes, not for each prefix on its own, and those groups are the ASes. Each AS has a globally unique number (the ASN) used both in routing exchanges and as the AS's identifier. The RFC also notes that traffic in the two directions need not take the same path. This is called asymmetrical routing, and it should be used with caution and only when necessary.
sections.eli5: An AS is a group of networks that all follow one set of traffic rules. Each group gets its own number so neighbors know who is who.

sections.title: Do I Need an AS?
sections.content:
The RFC gives three criteria. First, an AS must be used to exchange external routing information with other ASes through an exterior routing protocol, which at the time was BGP. But exchanging external routing information alone does not create the need for one.

Second, as a general rule, place as many prefixes as possible inside one AS, provided they all follow the same routing policy. Third, an AS is only needed when your routing policy differs from that of your border gateway peers.

The RFC also warns against common errors. An AS must have only one routing policy, without exception, so it is wrong to use an AS as a label for everything under one administrative roof. Creating an AS for its own sake, or one AS per classful network, is to be avoided. The ideal is one prefix, containing many longer prefixes, per AS.
sections.eli5: You only need your own badge number if you play by different rules than your neighbors. If you follow the same rules as your provider, you can share its number.

sections.title: Sample Cases
sections.content:
The RFC works through three situations.

  • Single-homed site, single prefix: no separate AS. The prefix goes into the provider's AS because it has exactly the same routing policy as the provider's other customers.
  • Single-homed site, multiple prefixes: again no separate AS; the prefixes go into the provider's AS.
  • Multi-homed site: an AS is required. Here multi-homed means connected to more than one service provider, each with its own routing policy. The site's prefixes should form a single AS distinct from its providers' ASes.

The multi-homed case is described as ALMOST THE ONLY case where an operator should create its own AS number, and the site should have the facilities to run protocols such as BGP4. A single site or part of a site may occasionally need a policy different from its provider's, in which case a separate AS must be created, but the RFC says this is rare and should almost never happen.
sections.eli5: If you only buy from one shop, you can use the shop's badge. If you buy from two shops and want to pick between them, you need your own badge.

sections.title: Other Factors and Speculation
sections.content:
Several reasons people give for creating an AS are treated with caution. Geography, acceptable use policy compliance and topology can influence the decision, but all too often they are used without asking whether an AS adds routing policy information the rest of the Internet needs.

Planning to connect to a second provider later is not enough of a reason to create an AS early. The AS number space is finite, and the small amount of re-engineering needed when a second provider is added is considered a natural step in transition. The RFC also notes that AS application forms historically made no reference to routing policy, and suggests that future forms point to this document to show when an AS is needed.

The speculation section adds two ideas. If many customers are multi-homed between the same two large providers, it may make sense to place them in one AS, but only if practical and fully coordinated. And sites should not be forced into a separate AS just so someone else can make AS-based policy decisions, although the final decision stays with the operators managing the prefixes and ASes.
sections.eli5: Do not ask for a badge just because you might need one someday. Badge numbers run out, and getting one later is not hard.

sections.title: One Origin AS and IGP Tags
sections.content:
Generally a prefix should belong to only one AS, because at each point in the Internet there can be exactly one routing policy for traffic destined to a prefix. For a prefix used in peering between two ASes, a conscious decision should be made about which AS it lives in. With aggregation, a prefix may appear to reside in more than one AS, for example when using the BGP AS_SET attribute, but this is the exception.

Many router vendors ask for an identifier to tag interior gateway protocol (IGP) processes. That tag does not need to be globally unique and is never seen by exterior routing protocols. If you already run an exterior protocol, using your AS number as the tag is reasonable; otherwise the private use range is acceptable. Merely running an IGP is not grounds for registering an AS number. With BGP4, the IGP must be able to carry classless routes; the RFC names OSPF and IS-IS as examples.
sections.eli5: Each street should belong to one neighborhood, so everyone agrees where to send the mail. Your own internal labels do not need a worldwide badge.

sections.title: AS Number Space and Reserved Numbers
sections.content:
The AS number space is finite. When the RFC was written it was a 16-bit integer, limited to 65535 unique numbers. Some 5,100 ASes had been allocated and a little under 600 were actively routed in the global Internet. The authors conclude that if the criteria are followed there is no immediate danger of exhaustion, and they expected IDRP, which has no fixed limit on the size of its routing domain identifier, to be deployed before it became an issue.

The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) reserved the block 64512 through 65535 for private use. Those numbers are not to be advertised on the global Internet.
sections.eli5: There are only so many badge numbers, so we should not waste them. A block at the end is set aside for private games that stay inside your own club.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are few security concerns about selecting ASes. AS number to owner mappings are public knowledge (in WHOIS), and the authors argue that trying to change that would only confuse the people trying to route IP traffic on the Internet.
sections.eli5: Who owns which badge number is public, like a phone book. Hiding it would only confuse everyone.
